At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One! Within this assembly, is there anyone who..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this samādhi, do they also attain the eighty-four thousand gates of the pāramitās, as well as the various gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī?
The Buddha told King Nanda:

"In this assembly there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained this samādhi; they are also able to enter the eighty-four thousand pāramitās, as well as the various gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī."
All these bodhisattvas shall, within this Bhadrakalpa, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with the exception of the four Tathāgatas who have already attained Buddhahood in this kalpa.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I pray that you will show compassion and proclaim the names of these bodhisattvas; it will bring great benefit, bringing peace and security to the world and benefiting devas and humans. It shall protect the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure for a long time, and protect future bodhisattvas by manifesting the light of the Dharma, ensuring their resolve for the unsurpassed path never grows weary.”
The Buddha told King Nanda:
“Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
“So be it, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear it.”

We, the disciples, from immeasurable kalpas until this very day, have created various kinds of karma during that interval.
Indeed, karma can adorn the realms of existence wherever one may be; therefore, through reflection, we seek liberation from the world.
Therefore, the karmic retributions of the six realms are diverse and their forms and species differ; one should know that all are produced by the power of karma.
Thus, among the Buddha’s ten powers, the power of karma is most profound.
Ordinary worldlings often give rise to doubts and suspicions regarding this matter, asking:
"For what reason is it so?
For they observe in the world that those who practice virtue encounter misfortune at every turn.
Those who commit evil find their undertakings coincidentally successful, leading them to say:
"In this world, there is no distinction between good and evil.
Such calculations are all due to an inability to deeply penetrate the principles of karma.
Why is this so? For it is stated in the Sūtra:
"There are three kinds of karma."
What are the three?
First, retribution in the present life; second, retribution in the next life; third, retribution in subsequent lives.
Regarding karma with retribution in the present life: one performs good or evil deeds in the present and receives the retribution in the present body.
Karma to be experienced in the present life refers to performing wholesome or unwholesome deeds in this life and receiving their retribution in the next life.

Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives refers to performing wholesome or unwholesome deeds either in the past throughout immeasurable lifetimes, or in this very life, and receiving their retribution either in this life, or in a future life.

"As for those who previously committed evil yet now appear to be flourishing, this is due to the ripening of wholesome karma from past lives—whether as retribution in the present life or in future lives; it is for this reason that they enjoy these fruits of happiness in the present.
How could this have anything to do with performing various evil deeds in the present and receiving a favorable reward?"

When a person who practices virtue experiences suffering in the present life, it is because the retributive effects of evil karma from past lives—whether manifesting in this lifetime or in subsequent ones—have ripened; thus, the power of their current roots of goodness is too weak to dispel it, and they consequently receive this bitter retribution.
How could this possibly be related to performing good deeds in the present, which would instead attract an evil retribution?
How is this known to be so?

We observe in the present world that those who perform wholesome deeds are praised by others and respected by others; therefore, we know that they will inevitably bring about pleasant fruits in the future.
Since there have been such evil karmas in the past, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach that one should draw near to virtuous friends and together perform repentance.
Regarding the attainment of the Way, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) provides complete benefit.
For this reason, disciples, today with utmost sincerity, we take refuge in all Buddhas.

We, the disciples, from beginningless time until this very day, have accumulated evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and committed transgressions that fill the heavens and the earth. In casting off one body and receiving another, we were neither aware nor cognizant of our actions; we have committed the five heinous crimes, bound by deep and heavy defilements and the karma of the Avīci hell;
we have become icchantikas, severing the roots of goodness;
and we have lightly slandered the Buddha’s words, maligning the Vaipulya sutras.
The karma of destroying the Three Jewels and subverting the True Dharma;
the karma of not believing in sin and merit, giving rise to the ten unwholesome actions;
and the karma of delusion and ignorance that leads one away from truth and back toward error.
The karma of being unfilial toward one's two parents and acting with perverse contrariness;
the karma of treating teachers and elders with contempt and lacking in ritual respect;
and the karma of being untrustworthy and unrighteous toward friends.
Or they create karma that constitutes fourfold, sixfold, or eightfold obstructions to the Noble Path;
they violate the five precepts and destroy the karma of the eightfold fast;
and they frequently commit transgressions against the five categories and seven groups of offenses.
The precepts of an upāsaka involve heavy and light defiled karma;
or the bodhisattva precepts cannot be kept pure, such that the preparatory and subsequent stages of one's practice, as described, defile the Brahma-conduct;
or there is no monthly observance of the six fast days, which constitutes the karma of indolence.
Observing the three long periods of fasting year after year, yet not constantly cultivating one's practice;
the three thousand codes of dignified conduct, yet failing to act in accordance with the Dharma;
the eighty thousand rules of discipline, yet committing subtle offenses.
They do not cultivate the karma of bodily and mental precepts;
they perform the sixteen kinds of unwholesome disciplinary acts;
they neither uproot nor rescue, lacking the karma of protection and refuge.
The karma of harboring jealousy and lacking the means to transcend it;
the karma of being partial toward enemies and kin;
and the karma of indulging in the five desires without weariness or renunciation.
Or, due to clothing and food, gardens, groves, and ponds, one gives rise to dissolute and idle occupations;
or, in the prime of youth, one indulges unrestrainedly in sensual desires, creating a multitude of sinful karmas;
or, through wholesome yet outflowing (sāsrava) deeds, one dedicates them toward the three realms of existence, thereby obstructing supramundane karma.
Such karmic actions as these are immeasurable and boundless; today I reveal them and repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly.

“May we disciples, by virtue of the merit and goodness arising from this repentance of all karma of the uninterrupted [sins], vow that in every birth and every lifetime, we shall extinguish the five heinous crimes and eliminate the delusions of the icchantika. As for such light and heavy transgressions, from this day forward until we reach the site of enlightenment, we solemnly vow never again to commit them.”
Constantly practicing supramundane, pure, and wholesome dharmas;

diligently maintaining the conduct of the Vinaya and guarding one’s dignified demeanor like a sea-crosser cherishing a life-preserving float; making the six perfections and four immeasurables the foremost of one's constant practice; causing the categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom to become increasingly bright and clear; swiftly accomplishing the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses; possessing great compassion and the three mindfulnesses; and always delighting in wondrous wisdom to attain the eight masteries.

Disciples, we have now collectively repented for all karmic actions in their general aspects; we shall now proceed to repent for each one individually in its specific aspects. Whether general or specific, coarse or subtle, light or heavy, confessed or unconfessed—may all these categories, following their respective kinds, be entirely extinguished."

Regarding the repentance for specific transgressions (*biexiang chan*): first repent for the three [misdeeds] of the body, next repent for the four [misdeeds] of the mouth, and for all other obstacles, prostrate yourself in succession.
As for the three karmas of the body, the first is killing; as clarified in the sutras, one may take oneself as a metaphor: "Do not kill, do not wield the staff."

Although there is a distinction between birds and beasts, their preservation of life and dread of death are one and the same in principle. If one investigates these sentient beings, from time immemorial they have been one's own parents, brothers, or members of the six classes of kin. Due to the causes and conditions of karma, they transmigrate through the six realms, passing from birth to death and changing form and retribution until they no longer recognize one another. To now inflict harm upon them and devour their flesh is the height of injury to compassion. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"If one obtains other food, one should regard it as eating the flesh of one's own child during a time of famine; how much more so should one treat this fish and meat?"
He further said:
"To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase various meats with money—both are evil karmas; upon death, one will fall into the Raurava Hell."
Thus we know that the sin of killing and devouring is deeper than rivers and seas, and more grievous than hills and mountains.
Yet, from time immemorial, we disciples have failed to encounter virtuous friends; all this is due to these very karmic deeds.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The sin of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or as hungry ghosts to undergo suffering.

If they are born among animals, they will receive the bodies of tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, hawks, or falcons; or they will receive the bodies of venomous snakes, vipers, scorpions, and the like, constantly harboring evil intent; or they will receive the bodies of deer, bears, brown bears, and the like, constantly dwelling in fear."
"If one is born among humans, one will receive two kinds of retributions: first, being frequently ill; second, having a short lifespan.
Since there are such immeasurable and various evil retributions for killing and eating [living beings], [one should refrain from it].
Therefore, disciples, today with utmost sincerity, we take refuge in all Buddhas.

We disciples, from time immemorial until this very day, having possessed this mind-consciousness, have constantly harbored cruel and poisonous thoughts, devoid of compassion. Whether through greed we have committed killing, or through anger, ignorance, or pride; whether by employing malicious means, vowing to kill, wishing to kill, or using incantations to kill;
whether by breaking dikes and draining lakes and ponds, burning mountains and forests, hunting and fishing;

or by setting fires driven by the wind, releasing hawks and dogs to pursue game, thereby harming all living beings—such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless. Today, with utmost sincerity, we repent them all.
Some use cages, snares, pits, traps, spears, halberds, bows, and crossbows to shoot and strike birds and wild beasts;

others use nets, weirs, and hooks to measure the depths of the water for fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, shrimp, clams, snails, and other moisture-dwelling creatures, leaving no place for those of the land, water, or air to hide or flee.
Or they raise chickens, pigs, cattle, sheep, dogs, boars, geese, and ducks to provide for their own kitchens.

Or one may purchase others for slaughter, causing their cries of distress to end before they have ceased, their feathers and fur to fall out, their scales and shells to be mangled, their bodies and heads to be severed, and their flesh and bones to be crushed; they are flayed, split, butchered, and carved, roasted, steamed, boiled, and grilled—inflicting cruel and agonizing harm upon the innocent. Yet this brings only momentary gratification, and the flavor gained by the mouth is but meager, lasting no longer than three inches of the tongue’s root.
Nevertheless, the retribution for such sin will bring calamity and suffering for eternal kalpas.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with the utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, I have caused the abortion of fetuses or the destruction of eggs, used poisons or sorcery to injure and kill sentient beings, tilled the soil and dug the earth, cultivated fields and gardens, raised silkworms and boiled cocoons—killing and injuring in great abundance;
or I have beaten and struck mosquitoes and gadflies, or crushed and bitten fleas and lice.
Some burn away refuse and clear drainage ditches, thereby harming all living beings;
some eat fruits and seeds;
or they recklessly kill sentient beings for the sake of grain, water, or vegetables.
Some burn firewood or expose lamps and candles, thereby killing various insects;
some consume sauces or vinegar without checking for moving life;
or they pour out hot water, drowning ants and other small creatures.

Thus, throughout all four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—we have constantly harmed and killed subtle and minute sentient beings, whether flying through the air or dwelling upon the earth.
We disciples, with the obscured consciousness of ordinary worldlings, have failed to perceive or take heed; today, with utmost sincerity, we repent for all of this.

"Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, the disciples have, through various evil means such as whips, staves, shackles, fetters, interrogation, beating, hurling, trampling with hands and feet, binding, caging, and depriving of water and grain, caused suffering to sentient beings."

Today, with utmost sincerity, we all perform repentance. We pray that by virtue of the merit arising from this repentance for our sins of killing and other transgressions, may we, throughout all future lives, attain a vajra-body and infinite lifespan; may we forever be free from enmity and hatred, harbor no intent to kill, and regard all sentient beings as our only child. Should we encounter those in peril or urgent distress, may we not spare our own bodies or lives but employ skillful means to rescue and liberate them. Thereafter, may we preach the subtle and wondrous True Dharma, so that all sentient beings—merely by beholding our forms or shadows—may receive peace and happiness, and merely by hearing our names or voices, may all their terrors be dispelled. Having finished this repentance and making these vows, we take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

Disciples, from time immemorial until this very day, we have either stolen the wealth and treasures of others, seizing them by force with blades raised;

Or they pilfer and embezzle taxes and assessments, steal customs duties at the passes, conceal public levies and contributions, and hide or evade corvée labor.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

Whether they were objects belonging to the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha; or property intended for the Saṃgha of the four quarters; or taken by theft or used through negligence, or withheld from return due to relying on one's power;

or borrowed personally or lent to others, or exchanged on loan and subsequently forgotten; or whether the property of the Triple Gem was confused and used indiscriminately; or whether communal goods such as grain, firewood, salt, soybeans, sauce, vinegar, vegetables, fruits, money, silk, bamboo, wood, brocades, banners, canopies, incense, flowers, oil, or candles were used according to my own whims or desires, either for my personal use or given away to others; [I now repent all such deeds].

Or plucking flowers and fruits offered to the Buddha, using the property of the Sangha’s garlands, or misappropriating the wealth of the Triple Gem for one's own private benefit—such offenses are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

"Furthermore, from beginningless time until this very day, whether acting as friends, teachers, monks, fellow students, parents, brothers, or other six types of close relatives, we have lived and resided together, and in all matters of necessity, we have deceived one another;

or, as neighbors and nearby residents, we have moved our fences, expanded our walls to encroach upon others' dwellings, altered boundary markers, changed landmarks, and seized their fields and gardens; or, under the guise of public business while pursuing private ends, we have usurped people's shops and marketplaces, as well as their rural estates."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, I have perhaps besieged cities and destroyed towns, burned villages and demolished stockades, stolen and sold free people, or enticed away the servants of others;

or again, I have unjustly oppressed innocent people, causing their spirits to be crushed, their bodies to be wounded by blades or shackled in vain fetters, their family estates to be scattered, and their kin to be separated by birth, dispersed to different regions, and severed from one another by life and death. Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

"Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, whether engaged in commerce and trade, or in the business of shops and markets, we have used light scales and small measures, reduced dimensions by a fraction of an inch, stolen grains by the *fen* and *xun*, and deceived others regarding *gui* and *he*. We have substituted coarse goods for fine ones and short items for long ones, employing a hundred kinds of clever deceptions in our hope for even the slightest profit."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, I may have breached walls or leaped over fences, blocked roads to plunder, defaulted on debts and interest, betrayed trust and violated agreements, or practiced deceit with my face while harboring different intentions in my heart and mouth;
or I may have used unrighteous means to seize and rob spirits, deities, birds, beasts, and all beings of the four modes of birth.

Or they resort to false pretenses such as fortune-telling and physiognomy to seize people's wealth and treasures; in this way, they even seek profit through profit, pursuing it wickedly and excessively, without satiety or contentment.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we repent them all.

"We pray that by virtue of the merit arising from this repentance for the sins of robbery and theft, our disciples, in birth after birth, may obtain wish-fulfilling jewels. May the seven treasures, exquisite garments, the nectar of a hundred flavors, and various medicinal decoctions rain down constantly. Whatever is required according to one's will shall arrive immediately upon thought. May all sentient beings be free from thoughts of stealing or plundering; may all be able to have few desires and know contentment, neither being addicted nor defiled, always delighting in giving, practicing the path of urgent relief, and regarding their own heads, eyes, marrow, and brains as they would spit or snot, thereby dedicating [this merit] toward the fulfillment of the *dāna-pāramitā*."

Or the tongue craves delicious flavors—fresh, savory, sweet, and rich—the blood and flesh of sentient beings, which nourish the four great elements only to further increase the root of suffering, giving rise to unrighteous thoughts.
Regarding the body’s delight in flowers, brocades, embroidery, silks, and gauzes, as well as all fine, smooth textures and garments of the seven treasures—these give rise to unrighteous thoughts;
or the mind is filled with many distracted thoughts, such that every contact and orientation deviates from the Dharma.
These six types of perception lead to the commission of particularly grave offenses.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly.

“May we disciples, by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance for sins such as lustful desire, be spontaneously born in every life and age without passing through a womb; may we be pure and radiant, with the marks and signs of excellence shining brilliantly; may our six sense-faculties be clear and open, and our intelligence sharp and discerning; may we thoroughly understand that affection and love are like shackles, and contemplate these six sense-objects as being like illusions and transformations; may we develop a definitive revulsion toward the realms of the five desires, such that even in dreams no perverse thoughts arise, and neither internal nor external causes and conditions can ever move us.”

By the merit of this repentance of the eye faculty, may these eyes see through to the ten directions the pure Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, without perceiving them as dualistic phenomena.

I vow that by the merit of this repentance of the faculty of hearing, may these ears always hear the True Dharma taught by the Buddhas and Sages of the ten directions, and may I practice in accordance with those teachings.

By the merit of this repentance of the olfactory faculty, may this nose always perceive the fragrance of the Accumulated Merit, the fragrance of entering the stage of Dharma, and may it abandon the impure stench and filth of birth and death.

By the merit of this confession of the faculty of the tongue, I vow that this tongue shall always partake of the food of Dharma-joy and the sustenance of dhyāna-bliss, never again craving the flavor of the flesh and blood of sentient beings.

By the merit of this confession of the faculty of the body, may this body don the robe of the Tathāgata, wear the armor of patience, lie upon the bed of fearlessness, and sit upon the seat of the four dhyānas.

By the merit of this repentance of the mental faculty, may this mind accomplish the ten perceptions and penetrate the five sciences; may it deeply contemplate the principle of the equality of emptiness within the two truths, and from the wisdom of skillful means, give rise to the ten sublime practices; may it enter the stream of Dharma, increasing in clarity with every thought-moment, and manifest the Tathāgata’s great patience of non-arising.
Having finished repenting and making vows, I take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

Homage to all Buddhas of the past, present, and future, throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as far as the limits of empty space. I take refuge and repent:
With a sincere heart, I repent!
Having completed the repentance for all karmic obstructions, we next repent for all obstacles regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

As the Buddha said in the sutras: "A human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha-Dharma is difficult to hear; the assembly of monks is difficult to encounter; faith is difficult to give rise to; the six sense faculties are difficult to possess in full; and virtuous friends are difficult to find."

"Now, through the roots of goodness we have cultivated together in past lives, we have obtained this human body with all six faculties intact; furthermore, having encountered virtuous friends, we have been able to hear the True Dharma."

In the interim, we were likewise unable to exert ourselves with wholehearted diligence; fearing that we might sink into myriad sufferings for all eternity in the future with no hope of escape, we today reach a state of profound shame and remorse, and thus confess and repent for it all.
"Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, our minds have been constantly shrouded by ignorance and our intentions obstructed by afflictions;
upon seeing the images of the Buddha, we were unable to show them full-hearted reverence;
we held the Sangha in contempt, harmed our virtuous friends, destroyed stupas and temples, burned images, and shed the blood of the Buddha."

Or they may reside in magnificent halls themselves while placing sacred images in lowly and filthy places, subjecting them to smoke, sun exposure, wind, rain, and dew, as well as dust and filth; or allowing them to be damaged by sparrows and rats, sharing their quarters with them without ever showing reverence;
or leaving the bodies of the images exposed without ever adorning them;
or shielding them from lamps and candles, or locking away the temple buildings to obstruct the Buddha’s radiance.

I now repent of all such transgressions. Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, regarding the Dharma, I have handled scriptures with impure hands; I have locked them away in chests and boxes where they were eaten by insects or rotted; I have allowed their bindings and rollers to fall off and their sections to lose their order; I have permitted seams to come undone, pages to be omitted or misplaced, and paper or ink to tear and break; and I have failed to repair them myself or to propagate them.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; therefore, disciples, today with utmost sincerity, take refuge in all Buddhas.

I take refuge in and repent before all Buddhas of the past, present, and future, throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as far as the limits of space.
With a sincere heart, I repent!
We, the disciples, from immeasurable kalpas until this very day, throughout that interval, have committed transgressions according to our minds and incurred faults following our impulses;
these matters have been contrary to the Way, leading us to commit many offenses wherever we go;
we have traversed the paths of the three obstructions and entered the forest of the eight heterodoxies.
Ascending the platform of afflictions and mounting the palace of ignorance,
they cause the pond of dhyāna to dry up, so that the lotus of wisdom cannot be drawn forth;
the tree of precepts is withered and broken, so that the flowers and leaves of samādhi do not grow.
In the prime of life, they were heedless and committed immeasurable and boundless transgressions;
with ignorance shrouding their minds, they committed manifold sins;
the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes numbered like dust motes and grains of sand.
The transgressions of the three karmas and six sense faculties are difficult to describe in full.
Due to these obstacles of sin, one's misfortunes will afflict future lives; as the seeds of retribution ripen in a subsequent birth, one shall fall into hell.
Thereupon, ox-headed demons let out thunderous roars as they drag [the beings] toward the mountain of blades; the hell-wardens frown as they drive them up the sword-trees.
Day and night, they die ten thousand deaths and live ten thousand lives;
their flesh is consumed within the cauldrons of boiling water, and their bones are shattered beside the copper pillars.
Iron-beaked birds peck at their eyes;
copper-clawed beasts with sharp fangs tear at their bodies and heads;
they are boiled, roasted, and scorched upon freezing ice and agonizing coals.
Pounded by mortars, ground by stones, plowed by oxen, and split by saws—such agonies are immeasurable and boundless, beyond full description and beyond full narration.
We, the disciples, now before the Buddhas, Dharma, and Sangha of the ten directions, openly confess all our karmic obstructions and transgressions.
With a sincere heart, I repent for all transgressions already committed, praying that they may be eliminated through this confession;
as for those not yet committed, from this day forward, I shall reform my past ways and cultivate myself for the future, never daring to commit them again.
Having finished repenting and making vows, one takes refuge and pays homage to the Triple Gem.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, the names of the Buddhas who appear in the world are as follows.

If a person hears the names of these thousand Buddhas, they will not fear error and shall certainly attain nirvana. All wise people who hear the names of these Buddhas should maintain a single-minded focus; they must not harbor negligence, but should practice with diligent effort.
If one loses these conditions, one will fall back into the evil realms and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

One who abides securely in the observance of precepts, accords with extensive learning, constantly delights in seclusion, and is fully endowed with profound patience, such a person shall be able to encounter a thousand Buddhas.

If one recites the names of these thousand buddhas, then the multitude of sins accumulated over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas will be extinguished. One will certainly attain the samādhis and supernormal powers of all buddhas, as well as unimpeded wisdom, various dharma-gates, various dhāraṇīs, and the manifold wisdom found in all scriptures; one will preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate. All of this should be sought and cultivated through this very samādhi.

One should practice a pure livelihood and not give rise to deception; remain free from fame and profit, and harbor no envy. Practice the six points of respectful harmony; one who practices in this way will swiftly attain the dharma of samādhi.
The Sutra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Present Bhadrakalpa.
